meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Of course I don't believe in it. But I understand that it brings you luck whether you believe in it or not'?
meta.ogDescription: A horseshoe anecdote pinned on Niels Bohr by 1956, retold many ways. No known Bohr writing has this wording, and Heisenberg gives the line to Bohr's neighbor.

answer.label: Not Niels Bohr’s documented words — a retold anecdote
answer.sourceLine: This is a polished retelling of a horseshoe anecdote credited to Bohr in print by 1956. Quote Investigator ↗ found no direct evidence in his writings. Wikiquote lists it as Disputed, and in Heisenberg’s account Bohr tells it about a neighbor.

source.heading: Where the anecdote actually appears

docMeta.dd: “The Wit Parade,” E. E. Kenyon, Cleveland Plain Dealer (The American Weekly), 30 Sept. 1956, p. 13
Not found in any documented account; a later paraphrase

source.excerpt: “Of course not,” replied the scientist. “But I understand it’s lucky whether you believe in it or not.”
trail: The earliest match known to Quote Investigator ↗ is a January 1956 item in the Swedish daily Svenska Dagbladet. It names Bohr, has an unnamed “curious American” ask about the horseshoe, and gives Bohr’s reply as “Of course not” in Swedish.

On 30 September 1956, E. E. Kenyon’s “The Wit Parade” column ran the English line “But I understand it’s lucky whether you believe in it or not” (ADS-L, 2013 ↗). Later retellings use “I’ve been told,” “I am told it works” and “they say it helps.”

In Werner Heisenberg’s Physics and Beyond, p. 92, as quoted on Wikiquote ↗, Bohr tells the story about a neighbor in Tisvilde who hung the horseshoe. The neighbor answers, “Of course not; but they say it helps even if you don’t believe in it.”
Quote Investigator concludes: “QI has not located any direct evidence in the writings of Niels Bohr.” Wikiquote puts the anecdote under Disputed on its Bohr page ↗.
source.excerptNote: The 1956 “Wit Parade” humor column, as transcribed by Quote Investigator. Its “I understand… whether you believe in it or not” is the closest early match to the popular line, which turns “Of course not” into “Of course I don’t believe in it” and “it’s lucky” into “it brings you luck.”

source.rightsNote: No identifiable work contains this exact wording. It is an anonymous modern paraphrase of a widely retold anecdote, so no rights status is asserted. The 1956 newspaper column and the later books that tell the story are separate works with their own rights.

author.name: Niels Bohr
author.heading: The name it’s pinned on
author.bio: Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist and one of the founders of quantum theory. Many neat sayings and anecdotes are credited to him. This one, about a horseshoe over a door, is told secondhand and is not found in his own writings.

cite.sourceCitation: Unsourced paraphrase. The anecdote is attached to Niels Bohr in Svenska Dagbladet (Stockholm), January 1956, p. 8, which is the earliest match known to Quote Investigator. The closest early English wording is E. E. Kenyon, “The Wit Parade,” Cleveland Plain Dealer (The American Weekly), September 30, 1956, p. 13. See Quote Investigator, “I Understand It Brings You Luck, Whether You Believe in It or Not,” October 9, 2013, https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/09/horseshoe-luck/.

copyAttribution: Often credited to Niels Bohr, but not in his writings: a later paraphrase of a horseshoe anecdote attached to him by 1956 (Quote Investigator).

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The horseshoe story is real folklore, but the speaker, the setting and the wording all change from one telling to the next. The exact line here is passed around as Bohr’s, for example on WIST Quotations ↗, which itself labels it “Attributed.”

items.why: Accounts from 1956 onward name him, but they are all secondhand and none is from his own writings. Quote Investigator ↗ says future evidence may clarify where the story came from and whether it is true.
In Heisenberg’s Physics and Beyond, as quoted on Wikiquote ↗, the horseshoe and the retort belong to a neighbor, and Bohr is only telling the story.
In lectures given in 1959 and reprinted in 1977, the Swiss psychiatrist C. A. Meier, first president of the C. G. Jung Institute, tells the story without naming the scientist (Quote Investigator ↗).
QI notes that in 1986 the Washington Post’s ombudsman, Joseph Laitin, printed a version with Einstein as the main figure (Quote Investigator ↗).
Wikiquote says the anecdote “possibly originated” with Goudsmit (Wikiquote ↗). QI notes that a 1973 anthology credits the story to Bohr via I. B. Cohen and S. A. Goudsmit.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is a smoothed-out retelling of a horseshoe joke that was attached to Niels Bohr by 1956. Quote Investigator found it in no writing by Bohr, and the earliest accounts do not use this wording (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why the story stuck to Bohr
lead: The joke pokes fun at a rational person hedging with a lucky charm, and pinning it on the man who helped build quantum theory makes the irony sharper. Some later tellings, including Pais’s and Heisenberg’s, set it at Tisvilde, Bohr’s country retreat, but they disagree on whose door it was. Others put it at his home, on his lab door, at his country cabin or, with Einstein, in Princeton.

The first known print versions, from 1956, are a Swedish newspaper item and an American humor column. Those are the kinds of outlets where anecdotes about famous people get tidied up and passed along. The sentence quoted today is smoother than any of the early versions.
context.pull: “But I understand it’s lucky whether you believe in it or not.” — humor column, 1956

sourcesVerified.claim: QI: the earliest match known to QI is Svenska Dagbladet, January 1956, p. 8, naming Bohr, with an unnamed 'curious American' visitor and the reply 'Of course not'
QI: Sept 30 1956 Cleveland Plain Dealer 'The Wit Parade' by E. E. Kenyon, p. 13: '"Of course not," replied the scientist. "But I understand it's lucky whether you believe in it or not."'
QI conclusion: 'QI has not located any direct evidence in the writings of Niels Bohr'; future evidence may clarify the story's origin and truth

QI: Meier's 1959 lectures (reprinted 1977) do not name the scientist; 1986 Washington Post ombudsman (Joseph Laitin) version features Einstein; a 1973 anthology credits it to Bohr via I. B. Cohen and S. A. Goudsmit

Wikiquote lists the horseshoe anecdote in Bohr's Disputed section (Pais 1986 p. 210; Sambursky 1974 p. 357), notes it was possibly originated by Samuel Goudsmit, and quotes Heisenberg's Physics and Beyond p. 92, where Bohr tells it about a Tisvilde neighbor: 'Of course not; but they say it helps even if you don't believe in it.'
ADS-L post by Garson O'Toole (Sept 4 2013) gives the 1956 Kenyon 'Wit Parade' wording and Meier's version with an unnamed 'world-famous scientist'
WIST Quotations gives the exact popular wording, labeled '(Attributed)', with variants and no primary source
